arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Banner argued the Sixth Amendment protects overnight conversations about testimony, including plea advice, evidentiary rulings, and perjury prevention. He said the line between strategy and testimony is unworkable and chills lawyers. He asked the Court to reverse.

Mr. Warthen argued trial courts may bar discussion of testimony during long breaks, relying on precedents like Geders and Perry. He said qualified orders balance constitutional rights with trial integrity. He asked the Court to affirm.

Mr. Barber argued a defendant has no right to discuss testimony midstream, and that qualified orders are constitutional. He said the Court should reject a categorical rule barring such orders in all courts.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case involves a Texas defendant whose trial judge barred him and his lawyer from discussing his testimony during an overnight recess. The lawyer could talk about trial strategy but not about the testimony itself. The defendant argues this violated his Sixth Amendment right to counsel. Texas says the order was constitutional.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A Texas trial court issued the order during the defendant's trial. State appellate courts upheld it. The defendant then asked the Supreme Court to review the case.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 5, lines 11-21
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 80, lines 47-7

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The defendant, Mr. Banner, argues the Sixth Amendment guarantees basic lawyer-client conversations, including reviewing testimony that already happened and preparing for the next day. He says a lawyer cannot advise a client about plea deals, evidentiary rulings, or perjury risks without discussing testimony.

Texas, Mr. Warthen, argues trial courts may bar counsel from managing ongoing testimony or discussing it altogether during long breaks. It relies on Supreme Court precedents allowing qualified orders to protect the integrity of cross-examination. It asks the Court to affirm the lower courts' rulings upholding the order.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The defendant argues the order effectively barred many kinds of discussion Texas now claims are permitted.He says defense lawyers will avoid any talk about testimony to avoid contempt. And That the majority rule in the United States already allows full discussion of testimony during overnight recesses.

Texas argues a defendant has no right to discuss testimony with counsel once that testimony has begun, just as any other witness cannot. It says qualified orders are constitutional and workable, and that the Court should not impose a categorical rule on all federal and state courts.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Thomas questioned what distinguishes coaching during testimony from coaching during a recess, and whether the order's standard was clear.
Chief Justice Roberts questioned how a prosecutor could probe what was discussed without intruding on attorney-client privilege, and asked what the lawyer told the defendant to say or change.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The ruling could shape how trial courts nationwide balance a defendant's right to counsel against the need to keep testimony untainted by coaching during breaks. It may determine whether qualified orders restricting testimony discussions are constitutional in federal and state courts.
